title: Scores, the Welcome window and the Top 10
kind: a build chapter: the windows every player sees before the map
one: You read the scores in `scores.txt`, and build the Welcome window. It shows the player's last and best scores, and a Top 10 board with one row for each player.

stages.title: See what the Welcome window shows

screens.title: Look at the Welcome window and the Top 10 board

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you will know what the Welcome window shows, and where each number comes from.
After a player logs in, the Welcome window opens. On the left is a white card with their avatar, a welcome message, their last score and their best score.

screenshot.alt: The Welcome window, with the player card on the left and the Top 10 board on the right
screenshot.cap: The Welcome window that you build in this chapter.

blocks.p: On the right is the Top 10 board. Each player is on it once, with their best score. Higher scores come first. Two equal scores go in A to Z order of username.
The player who is logged in has their own row in bold, on a pale gold background, so they can find themselves.
Every score comes from `scores.txt`, one score on each line: the username, the score and the date, with a bar `|` between them.

code.title: scores.txt: the first 3 lines
partLines: One score on each line
summitSeeker has finished 3 expeditions here. Only the best, 760, goes on the board.

screens.title: Check that your project is ready, and see the words this chapter uses

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you will know that your project has everything the Welcome window needs.

need: Your Log in window. It opens the Welcome window (`frmWelcome`) and remembers which player logged in (`Expedition.CurrentPlayer`) (chapter 6).
The file `scores.txt` in the Data folder inside bin\Debug, from `summit-ready-files.zip` (chapter 2).
Mix.Ordinal, which turns 1 into 1st, and the Sound class (chapter 2).
About 3 hours. Your ticks are kept, so you can stop at the end of any screen and come back later.

words: Convert.ToInt32
Turns text into a whole number. `Convert.ToInt32("250")` gives the number 250.
Dictionary
A collection that finds each value by a key, such as a player's best score by their username.
key
The value a Dictionary finds things by. Each key is in a Dictionary once only.
bubble sort
A way to put a list in order. It goes along the list again and again, swapping any two neighbours that are in the wrong order.
string.Compare
Compares two pieces of text for A to Z order. It gives a number below 0 when the first comes before the second.
ListView
A control that shows rows and columns, like a small table, with a picture at the start of each row.
ImageList
A control that holds pictures of the same size for another control, such as the ListView.
SubItems
The second, third and later columns of a ListView row.
Visible
A control with Visible set to false is not shown on the window.
DialogResult
Which button the player clicked in a MessageBox, such as Yes or No.
blocks.intro: You do not need to learn these words now. Where you first meet each one in the chapter, it has a dotted line under it. Hover over it or tap it to see what it means.

screens.title: Type LastScore and BestScore

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, ScoreFile can find a player's last score and their best score.
Both methods start at -1, which means no score. A real score is never below 0, so -1 is safe to use.

LastScore keeps the score from every line with the player's username. Lines are in the order they were saved, so the last one kept is the most recent. BestScore keeps a score only when it is higher than the best so far.

code.title: LastScore and BestScore
partLines: LastScore
Each matching line replaces `last`, so the last match is what comes back.
BestScore
`&&` means both must be true: the right player, and a higher score than `best`.

screens.title: Type the first half of TopTen: each player's best score

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, TopTen has an array, a numbered row of boxes, holding each player's best score once.
summitSeeker has 4 scores, but goes on the board once. So the first pass keeps one ScoreEntry for each player: their best. A [[Dictionary|1]] finds each player's best so far by their username.
The second pass copies the bests from the Dictionary into an array, ready to sort.

code.title: TopTen: the first half
partLines: The method
TopTen gives back an array of 10 places. An empty place is `null`.
Keep each player's best
A new username is added with its score. For a username already in the Dictionary, a higher score replaces the one kept.
Copy the bests into an array
`best.Count` is the number of players. `n` counts along the array as each best is copied in.

screens.title: Finish TopTen with a bubble sort, and type ComesBefore

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, TopTen gives back the 10 best players, highest score first.
A [[bubble sort|3]] goes along the array again and again. Each time two neighbours are in the wrong order, it swaps them. After enough passes, the whole array is in order.
A swap needs a spare variable, `keep`, so that neither value is lost.

code.title: TopTen: the sort and the first ten
partLines: The passes
Each pass carries the lowest score left to its place at the end, so each pass can stop one place sooner.
Swap two neighbours
If the second score should come before the first, the two swap places.
The first ten
The loop stops at 10 places, or at the end of the array if fewer than 10 players have scores.

glossary: Convert.ToInt32
Turns text into a whole number. `Convert.ToInt32("250")` gives the number 250.
Dictionary
A collection that finds each value by a key, such as a player's best score by their username.
key
The value a Dictionary finds things by. Each key is in a Dictionary once only.
bubble sort
A way to put a list in order. It goes along the list again and again, swapping any two neighbours that are in the wrong order.
string.Compare
Compares two pieces of text for A to Z order. It gives a number below 0 when the first comes before the second.
ListView
A control that shows rows and columns, like a small table, with a picture at the start of each row.
ImageList
A control that holds pictures of the same size for another control, such as the ListView.
SubItems
The second, third and later columns of a ListView row.
Visible
A control with Visible set to false is not shown on the window.
DialogResult
Which button the player clicked in a MessageBox, such as Yes or No.
